title: No. 20 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton & Madison)
paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON
The United Netherlands is a confederacy of republics, or rather of aristocracies, of a very remarkable texture, yet it confirms all the lessons drawn from those we have already reviewed.

The union is composed of seven coequal and sovereign states, and each state or province is itself a composition of equal and independent cities. In all important matters, not only the provinces but the cities must be unanimous.

The sovereignty of the Union is represented by the States-General, usually consisting of about fifty deputies appointed by the provinces. They hold their seats — some for life, some for six, three, and one years. From two provinces they continue in their appointments at the pleasure of those provinces.

The States-General has authority to enter into treaties and alliances; to make war and peace; to raise armies and equip fleets; to set quotas and demand contributions. In all these cases, however, unanimity and the approval of the constituents are required. They have authority to appoint and receive ambassadors; to execute treaties and alliances already made; to provide for the collection of duties on imports and exports; to regulate the mint, with provision for the rights of the provinces; and to govern as sovereigns the dependent territories. The provinces are restrained, except by general consent, from entering into foreign treaties; from establishing imposts harmful to others or charging their neighbors with higher duties than their own subjects. A council of state, a chamber of accounts, and five colleges of admiralty assist and strengthen the federal administration.

The executive magistrate of the union is the stadtholder, who is now an hereditary prince. His main weight and influence in the republic come from this independent title; from his great patrimonial estates; from his family connections with some of the chief potentates of Europe; and, perhaps more than all, from his being stadtholder in the several provinces as well as for the union. In that provincial role he appoints town magistrates under certain regulations, executes provincial decrees, presides when he pleases in the provincial tribunals, and has throughout the power of pardon.
As stadtholder of the union he has, however, considerable prerogatives.

In his political role he has authority to settle disputes between the provinces when other methods fail; to take part in the deliberations of the States-General and in their particular conferences; to give audiences to foreign ambassadors; and to keep agents at foreign courts for his own affairs.

In his military role he commands the federal troops, provides for garrisons, and in general regulates military affairs. He fills all appointments from colonels to ensigns, and the governments and posts of fortified towns.

In his marine role he is admiral-general and oversees and directs everything related to naval forces and other naval affairs. He presides in the admiralties in person or by proxy, appoints lieutenant-admirals and other officers, and establishes courts-martial whose sentences are not carried out until he approves them.
His revenue, apart from his private income, amounts to three hundred thousand florins. The standing army he commands consists of about forty thousand men.

Such is the nature of the celebrated Belgic confederacy, as drawn on parchment. What characteristics has practice stamped on it? Weakness in the government; discord among the provinces; foreign influence and indignities; a precarious existence in peace, and special calamities from war.
It was long ago observed by Grotius that nothing but his countrymen's hatred of the house of Austria kept them from being ruined by the vices of their constitution.

The union of Utrecht, says another respectable writer, places an authority in the States-General that seems sufficient to ensure harmony, but the jealousy in each province makes the practice very different from the theory.

The same instrument, says another, obliges each province to levy certain contributions; but this article never could, and probably never will, be carried out, because the inland provinces, which have little commerce, cannot pay an equal quota.

In matters of contribution, it is the practice to set aside the articles of the constitution. The danger of delay forces the consenting provinces to furnish their quotas without waiting for the others, and then to obtain reimbursement from the others, by deputations, which are frequent, or otherwise as best they can. The great wealth and influence of the province of Holland enable her to accomplish both these purposes.

More than once it has happened that deficiencies had to be ultimately collected at the point of the bayonet. This is practicable, though dreadful, in a confederacy where one of the members exceeds in force all the rest, and where several of them are too small to think of resistance. But it is utterly impractical in one composed of members several of which are equal to each other in strength and resources, and each capable of a vigorous and persevering defense.

Foreign ministers, says Sir William Temple, who was himself a foreign minister, evade matters taken ad referendum by tampering with the provinces and cities. In 1726, the treaty of Hanover was delayed by these means a whole year. Instances of a similar nature are numerous and well known.

In critical emergencies, the States-General is often forced to overstep its constitutional bounds. In 1688 they concluded a treaty on their own at the risk of their heads. The treaty of Westphalia in 1648, by which their independence was formally and finally recognized, was concluded without the consent of Zealand. Even as recently as the last treaty of peace with Great Britain, the constitutional principle of unanimity was set aside. A weak constitution must necessarily end either in dissolution, for lack of proper powers, or in usurpation of the powers needed for public safety. Whether the usurpation, once begun, will stop at the safe point or go on to the dangerous extreme, must depend on the circumstances of the moment. Tyranny has perhaps grown more often out of the assumptions of power, called for by pressing emergencies under a defective constitution, than out of the full exercise of the largest constitutional authorities.

Despite the calamities produced by the stadtholdership, it has been supposed that without his influence in the individual provinces, the causes of anarchy plain in the confederacy would long ago have dissolved it. "Under such a government," says the Abbe Mably, "the Union could never have lasted, if the provinces had not within themselves a spring capable of quickening their slowness and forcing them to think alike. This spring is the stadtholder." Sir William Temple remarks that "in the intervals of the stadtholdership, Holland, by her riches and authority, which drew the others into a kind of dependence, supplied the place."

These are not the only circumstances that have controlled the tendency to anarchy and dissolution. The surrounding powers impose an absolute necessity of union to a certain degree, while at the same time they nourish, by their intrigues, the constitutional vices that keep the republic always somewhat at their mercy.

True patriots have long lamented the fatal tendency of these vices. They have made no fewer than four formal experiments through EXTRAORDINARY ASSEMBLIES, convened for the special purpose, to apply a remedy. As many times their commendable zeal has found it impossible to UNITE THE PUBLIC COUNCILS in reforming the known, the acknowledged, the fatal evils of the existing constitution. Let us pause, my fellow-citizens, for a moment over this melancholy and warning lesson of history. With the tear that drops for the calamities brought upon mankind by their conflicting opinions and selfish passions, let our gratitude mix a prayer of thanks to Heaven for the providential harmony that has marked the consultations for our political happiness.
A plan was also conceived to establish a general tax administered by the federal authority. This too had its opponents and failed.

This unhappy people now seem to be suffering, from popular convulsions, from quarrels among the states, and from actual invasion by foreign arms, the crisis of their destiny. All nations have their eyes fixed on the dreadful spectacle. The first wish prompted by humanity is that this severe trial may issue in such a revolution of their government as will establish their union and make it the parent of tranquility, freedom, and happiness. The next is that the asylum under which we trust the enjoyment of these blessings will soon be secured in this country, may receive and console them for the catastrophe of their own.

I make no apology for having dwelt so long on these federal precedents. Experience is the oracle of truth, and where its responses are unequivocal they ought to be conclusive and sacred. The important truth it unequivocally pronounces in this case is that a sovereignty over sovereigns, a government over governments, a legislation for communities as opposed to individuals, is in theory a contradiction in terms, and in practice subverts the order and ends of civil polity by substituting VIOLENCE in place of LAW, or the destructive COERCION of the SWORD in place of the mild and salutary COERCION of the MAGISTRACY.
